cells.tense: The person is here at the present moment, pen in hand, holding a fairness level.
cells.act: count what the ending gave you
cells.ask: Take something that ended for you this year. Count what it gave you — the skill, what you can now do — and stop when the count is written. Nothing follows the number.
cells.core:
In a room made only of pattern, the scale reads clean. You can see what's owed, what was spent, whose side runs short, and the body keeps the tally without arguing.

What this balance is free to feed next is a harvest. Take one thing that ended — a role, a tie, a shape your week used to have — and count what it grew. Not the loss; the yield. What you can do now that you couldn't, what you paid for and kept. Put the count somewhere: on paper, in a note, wherever numbers go for you. When the count is down, quit counting. Something ended and it made something, and picking up the made thing is the offer here.
cells.sheetLine: You can see what was owed and hold it level.
cells.verb: weighing what is owed as if the scale could be seen
cells.place: a room where everything is pattern and none of it has weight

cells.tense: The person is braced at a fairness that hasn't happened yet and can't be written in.
cells.act: give a concrete piece of help and finish it
cells.ask: Choose one real thing a person near you needs done. Do all of it today, and when it's complete, walk away from it instead of watching.
cells.core:
You read fairness as pattern, so the near future is legible — who'll be short, what'll be owed, where the imbalance is heading. The bracing is against a bill not yet written, and it costs you one thing: your own settled matter stays unsettled, as if nothing should land until the account squares.

A brace doesn't take instruction, but hands can work. Pick one concrete need — a task, an errand, a hand someone needs — and give it completely today. Finish it, then leave it alone. Not because the future gets squared by it, but because your strength only shows itself when you spend it on something actual and then close the book on it.

cells.tense: The person is standing at a door that is already behind them, still facing it.
cells.act: show someone the way you found
cells.ask: Say the route you found through something hard, plainly, to whoever is standing where you once stood. Tell it as directions — turn here, then here — and stop when the directions stop.
cells.core:
There's a door behind you and you've stopped reaching for it. The route you found the hard way is still in you, filed as personal history, and the file sits shut. Fairness learned slowly tends to go unused, which is quiet work, not failure.

Here's the offer. You can see a way through that took years to find. Say it as a route — turn here, then here — to the person now standing where you once stood. Don't walk it for them. Don't tidy the story. When the directions run out, stop talking. The telling is what puts the finding back in your hands for good.

cells.tense: The person is already marking these lines, with the pen set down and no one watching.
cells.act: list the pulls on you and mark which are yours
cells.ask: Make two columns: every pull you feel toward a person or a duty, then which are actually yours. Draw the line between them, read the page once, and decide nothing.
cells.core:
You're marking these lines without a pen, and without a pen the borrowing goes unseen. Which fairness is actually yours, and which you carried in from a room you were in? What feels like conscience might be someone else's standard still billed to you, and the scale stays level either way, because the scale is right regardless of whose it is.

This week, put it on paper. One column: the pulls — toward a person, toward a duty, toward a standard you've kept a long while. The other: which are genuinely yours. Draw the line. Don't rank the list, don't act on it, don't show anyone. Read it back once and notice which column caught you off guard. That's the ask: the page, the marks, no verdict.
cells.sheetLine: The scale is level, and you didn't check whose.
